speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
(Translation.) I think it will be sufficient in order to satisfy my hon. friend, to state to the House the facts of the case, such as they have been brought to the notice of the Debates Committee. The facts will show that the claim put in by Mr. aiackay is a just one. Let me, then briefly review the facts in connection with that claim. At the beginning of last session air. aiackay was engaged as a translator by the committee, at the rate of $4 a day. That appointment was necessitated by the fact that air. Beaulieu, one of the officers of the regular translating staff was incapacitated owing to his poor health, from doing his work. Mr. Beaulieu, as my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville reminds me, was the former chief of the translating staff. As I said, the committee, finding it necessary to employ temporary assistance, sceured air. aiaekay's services and recommended that he be paid at the rate of $4 a day, which was equivalent for the work resulting from the session, to the sum of $1,000 which was the .salary then paid to the officers of the regular staff. Later^ on, and while air. Beaulieu was still unable' to discharge his duties, the position of the other officers of the permanent staff was changed, so far as their salary was concerned. Towards the close of the session of 1902, the House of Commons, acting upon the recommendation of the Select Committee appointed to supervise the official report of the Debates of this House, thought it proper to raise the salary of the officers of the translating staff from $1,000 to $1,500. Up to that time, they had received $1,000 per session ; but the House deemed it desirable to grant them a salary of $1,500 per annum, Instead of $1,000 per session. But it was not within the power of the committee to interfere with Mr. Mac-kay's position so far as the payments for his work was concerned. That gentleman, therefore, continued being employed temporarily on the staff, as the Hansard Committee was in hopes that Mr. Beaulieu would soon recover his health and resume his former occupation. The fact is that Mr. Beaulieu died three months after the close of the session, in the month of August, I think. Mr. Mackay being engaged only temporarily, we did not think it within our power to increase his salary, as the House had deemed it proper to do, upon the recommendation of the committee in the ease of the officers who compose the permanent staff, to whom the House had granted, for the future, a salary of $1,500. When the matter came up before the committee, and after the facts I have just referred to had been stated to them, namely, that Mr. Mackay had been engaged temporarily, they came to the conclusion that he was entitled to ask for the same remuneration as was paid to the other translators. After taking all the facts of the case into consideration, the committee deemed it but fair, and I think the House will agree with them, that Mr. Mac-

kay should be put upon a footing of equality with the rest of the translating staff.
My hon. friend from Labelle was anxious to know whether Mr. Mackay had gone through the test of an examination, thereby calling in doubt the competency of that gentleman. I must say that Mr. Mackay did not pass the examination which has been required within the last few years from all candidates who aspire to an appointment on the regular translating staff. The reason why the committee did not deem it proper to enforce the rule with that rigour the hon. gentleman seems to take exception to, is that Mr. Mackay was only appointed as a temporary substitute on the staff, in order to fill the vacancy created by Mr. Beaulieu's illness. I may further say, for the information of the House, that the committee did by no means depart from the rigour they have brought, within the past three or four years, to the discharge of their duty, in the matter of appointing translators on the regular staff, to fill such vacancies as may occur in that office. As concerns those appointments, there was no change made at all. Now, in the case of Mr. Mackay, his appointment was but a temporary one, the committee did not think it necessary to insist upon his passing such an examination as is required from candidates who aspire to be appointed on the regular staff. As I just remarked, the committee was then in hopes that Mr. Beaulieu would soon recuperate his health, and that explains why a permanent appointment was out of question. Under such circumstances, we deemed it fair and reasonable, seeing that Mr. Mackay had been discharging the same duties and doing the same work as the other translators, to ask the House to grant him a similar salary.
Such are the explanations I wanted to give to the House, and I hope they will prove satisfactory to my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). At all events, I may say that the members of the Debates Committee, after taking into consideration the facts I have just stated, have, without a dissentient voice, reached the conclusion that it was but fair and reasonable to make this recommendation to the House.

I may venture to suggest that, unless I am mistaken, when Mr. Mackay was appointed last year, as temporary substitute on the staff of the translators of the Debates during Mr. Beaulieu's illness, there were other candidates to that position who had passed their examination and had secured a certificate of competency. What I complain of is this, that the committee should have selected a man to fill Mr. Beaulieu's place who had not stood the test of an examination. I would be the last man to cast any blame upon the Hansard Committee for rigidly enforcing that rule, should they enforce* it indiscriminately in every case. X
may add that, whenever the committee stand in need of extra help for the translating staff, they should make their appointments from the ranks of those who have passed their examination, instead of going out of their way to select men whose only recommendation is that they have some pull and political influence at their back.

(Translation.) Let my hon. friend allow me to tell him that were the statement he has just made borne out by the actual facts, he would be fully justified in taking exception to such a condition of affairs, but the fact is that Mr. Mackay was engaged temporarily, before the committee had decided that any examinations should be held. Bill (No. 78) to amend the Militia Pension Act, 1901 (Minister of Militia and Defence), read the second time and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1,

Explain.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DE-FNCE (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden). The object of this Bill is to make the pension law for the permanent force similar to the law passed last year for the North-west Mounted Police ; that is to say, to enable a civil servant who is entitled under the Civil Service Superannuation Act to a pension, to participate in the benefits of the Superannuation Act for the time that he has been a member of the Civil Service and to the extent of the money which he has paid into the superannuation fund. It will be noticed that at the end of this proposed subsection 7, there is a reference to subsection 2 of section 5 of the Militia Pension Act. By that subsection it is enacted that in case an officer has not served the full length of time to entitle him to full superannuation, that is, in case he has not paid into the pension fund for the full length of 2J years, he will receive his pension subject to a deduction of 5 per cent per annum for the time he has not paid. This Bill provides that in case he has been a civil servant, he shall get the benefit of the 2i or 3 per cent, or whatever the rate may be, that he has paid under the Superannuation Act for the time that he has been a member of the civil service. To illustrate : suppose a man has been a civil servant for ten years, and has paid into the superannuation fund regularly during that time his 2} or 3 per cent, and is then appointed an officer in the permanent force or on the staff,

wliere lie becomes entitled to a pension under tlie Militia Pension Act. This Act will enable him to receive the full benefit of that payment for the ten years that he has been in the civil service, but he will be charged the difference between the amount he has paid into the superannuation fund and the 5 per cent charged under the Pension Act. The House passed precisely the same legislation last session in connection with the Pension Act for the Northwest Mounted Police.
I understand that he does not get anything under the Civil Service Superannuation Act ?
Nothing at all, and he would lose that but for this provision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I did not clearly understand the hon. minister. Under the Civil Service Pension Act an official pays two and a half per cent per year. Under the military system he would have to pay five per cent per year. On retiring from the military service, he gets the benefit of his civil service and military service, provided he pays the difference between the two percentages.
That is it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But the government loses the interest on the payments of the extra two and a half per cent during ten or fifteen years.
No, the government has the money.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: At the end of the term, tlie official pays the difference between two and a Half and five per cent. But if he had been all the time in the military service, he would have paid five per cent per year. Therefore, when he pays it in a lump sum at the end of the term, tlie government loses the interest, which may be quite a large amount.
That may be.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I do not quite understand how the concluding words of this section. ' Subject to the provisions of subsection two of section five,' can apply.

Take two cases. Suppose an officer has served twenty-five years, fifteen of which were before there was any Pension Act. During those fifteen years he paid nothing, but he will get his pension for the twenty-five years less deduction made of the premiums during the fifteen years, when he did not pay anything. Take another case. An officer has paid during ten years two and a half per cent into the civil service superannuation fund. During the next fifteen years he has paid five per
cent into the military service pension fund. Under this Bill, the intention is only to charge him the two and a half per cent during those ten years instead of the five.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The difficulty is this. Subsection two of section five of the present law provides for the case of an officer who in years gone by had no deduction whatever made from his pay. You strike an average of his pay and then make a deduction from his pension of five per cent on that average for every year during which he paid nothing. But how can you make this subsection apply to the present case, for you are not making a deduction of five per cent but only of two and a half per cent. You are applying a clause which deals specifically with one case to another and a different case.
I see the difficulty now, and will consider the matter. The five per cent is mentioned; and therefore, I think it would be desirable to draw up a clause long enough to state exactly what is intended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I think that would be the safer course.
I move that the Committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Before the Committee rises, I would like to understand the practical use of this amendment. I cau-not understand a civil servant who has been eight or ten years in the service getting an appointment on the staff or going into the permanent corps. Is it intended to have some ex post facto effect ? Is it to cover the case of some officer who has been in the department?

No. No particular case is aimed at, but I will give the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) a case such as would be covered by this. It is intended, in the near future, to transfer the stores branch of my department to the military side, making it an ordnance branch and putting it under military supervision. Now, we have in the stores branch civil servants who have been paying for years to the civil service fund. For instance, there is the head of that branch; and it would certainly be manifestly unfair to deprive him of the benefit of the money lie has paid into the superannuation fund.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What was passing through my mind was the question whether the converse will happen, and some officer will go from the permanent corps to the civil service ?

Not likely. The Pension Act is very much better here.

And he goes on, further down on the same page :
Nothwithstanding the increased convenience and shelter for immigrants at the East Selkirk building, the demands upon the accommodation of the hall here are very great, and are almost continuous. Large numbers of people daily visit the office on all conceivable kinds of business, and innumerable inquiries upon a great variety of subjects are answered by the staff of officials.
In the succeeding report of the department, that of 1901-02, we find Mr. Smart, the deputy minister speaking of the anticipated immigration. This is the report made by him on his return from England. At page 40, he said :
I may say that from all I have been able to gather I feel satisfied that the present year will see a very largely increased number of people remove to Canada from Great Britain and Ireland.
And in that same report, at page 125, we have Mr. Smith reporting as follows :
With the very large increase in the number of people passing through the hands of the staff connected with this office the duties of each official have been very materially increased, and I am pleased to know that the work has been carried on efficiently. With the possibility of a much greater increase of work, I beg to recommend the immediate erection of much larger office premises, and improvements in the buildings at Winnipeg, which are required to enable us to carry on our work with accuracy and rapidity.
So, Mr. Speaker, as far back as two years ago the reports of the officers of the department showed that they anticipated this influx of people into Manitoba andl the Northwest. And yet, what do we find ? Were any improvements ordered or any preparations made to receive these people ? Was any vote put in the estimates to provide money for buildings for their accommodation ? Why, Sir, in the estimates voted last year you will find that for public buildings for Manitoba there is the sum of $5,000. Tiie votes for some of the other provinces are as follows :	Nova Scotia, $61,-
500; New Brunswick, $33,000; Quebec, $103,000; Ontario, $222,800. And just $5,000 for public buildings for Manitoba, notwithstanding that officers of the Crown who were passing from one part of the empire to the other inducing people to come here, and notwithstanding that that officer of the department told the government what might be expected and warned them of what would be required to accommodate the people. Here the influx is upon the government, and the new-comers have to lie upon the floors of the station in Winnipeg.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, who I have no doubt sympathize with these people, if you consider the government have done what they should do in this matter, if you think they have placed a sufficient sum in the estimates for public buildings in Manitoba, under those conditions. I think, Sir,

you will agree with me that the members of the government who are responsible for this, when they lie upon their downy beds sleeping the sleep of the just and the righteous-whatever opinion we may have of them on this side of the House-I think you will agree with me that they must feel some remorse when they think of these poor people whom they are inducing to come into that country, and whom we are anxious to see come there ; and that they should have made some provision for them instead of allowing them to lie on the floor. I think the government should have some regard for these men and for their wives and children, and have made some better provision for their accommodation in the estimates, instead of spending so many thousands in various parts of the Dominion, largely for political purposes. Now, I think I am justified in bringing this matter to the attention of the government. I look across the House and see the premier sitting there, who, I believe to be a conscientious man, and who, when it comes to a matter of his fellowman, can be depended upon; I believe I can appeal to him to see to it that whoever is responsible for this condition of affairs will immediately take steps to remedy them. People are coming into our midst by the thousands, and I think it would be well for the premier, or for the minister who is responsible for that department, to see that his officers do everything that is possible to make these immigrants comfortable, so that we who come from the west may not have to make such complaints. We are delighted to see so large a number of people coming there, and we are going to do all we possibly can to make it pleasant and profitable for them. But we do not think that the government, under the circumstances, have done what they should have done, and we now lay the case before them and make a demand that they should meet the emergency and treat these people as they deserve.

The question that has been brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) is, I think, one of very great importance, and one that cannot be too strongly pressed upon the attention of the government. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) and the members supporting the government, have taken a great deal of credit to themselves for their so-called vigorous immigration policy, and have endeavoured to leave the impression throughout the country that it is largely owing to some new features in their policy that we have had this large influx of people coming to our shores the last two or three years. Now, every intelligent man is aware of the fact that this influx is largely owing to the splendid crops with which Providence has blessed that country during the last few years, it is largely owing to the fact 36
that over one hundred million bushels of grain have been raised in that western country during the year 1902. These things have done more to give our country a world-wide reputation than all the immigration agents in the service of the government. If the government are so anxious to take to themselves the credit of these people coming into Canada, they must also bear whatever blame attaches to them if these people are not properly looked after and afforded proper accommodation for their necessities. As my hon. friend from Macdonald has pointed out, the influx of people coming to our shores was not unexpected, and therefore the neglect of making proper accommodation for them is inexcusable. My hon. friend has pointed out that the Deputy Minister of the Interior, in his report, one or two years ago, anticipated this large immigration to Canada; the minister himself in his speeches has declared that although we had been blessed with a large influx of population the last year, it was nothing compared to the population that would come in, not only from the United States but from the British Isles, during the coming year. The deputy minister has been visiting Great Britain during the past winter, and in interviews reported in the public press of this country, papers irrespective of politics, we have been led to believe that a very large population would flock into Canada during the present year. I say therefore there is no excuse for the government in neglecting to make ample provision for their accommodation. Already in the beginning of the season we see 5,000 per week going into that western country, and we who live in the west are aware that the hotel accommodation in the city of Winnipeg is entirely inadequate to meet the demands of the travelling public for the last year or two. People have been turned away night and day at the hotels and boarding houses, all places of accommodation have been more than filled; and now we find these people compelled to sleep in the waiting room of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) brought to the attention of the House the other day another matter of prime importance in connection with the accommodation afforded for these people in the railway cars in which they are travelling through western Canada. He did not blame the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for that condition, but he largely blamed the government of the day. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company are, in this instance, deserving of every credit, no blame can be attached to them, they have done their utmost to accommodate their travellers. and have thrown open their public buildings. The blame therefore rests entirely on the Department of Immigration and the minister who is at the head of that department. Now, it is stated that we may expect this immigration to continue for



weeks and months. I understand that the deputy minister, who has just returned to Canada from England, states that passages have been booked for hundreds and thousands of immigrants for the next five or six weeks. It is evident that the government should have made some preparation for these people, but when we look at our estimates for the present year we find for the whole province of Manitoba a sum of only $5,000 for public buildings. Now we have had evidence of money being spent in other parts of the Dominion, thousands afd thousands of dollars are being voted for public buildings in every other province of the Dominion. We have seen L'Assomp-tion, a little village whose post office revenue is only $964, given a post office to cost $15,000; whereas in the whole province of Manitoba only $5,000 is voted for public buildings. This is something that should not be, especially in the important city of Winnipeg, the gateway of the west, the headquarters and distributing point of all these immigrants. Something should have been done to erect public buildings, especially immigration halls, where these people would have had proper accommodation. I noticed an article in a paper the other day which stated that the Winnipeg correspondent of the London ' Mail ' had sent over word that there was also a great congestion in the town of Saskatoon, in the Northwest Territories. While that has been denied by Mr. Preston, who was not on the ground and knows nothing whatever of the circumstances, still even if there were no truth in that report, there certainly is a congestion in Winnipeg, as evidenced in all the papers of that city irrespective of politics. We have been spending some half a million dollars for immigration purposes to attract people to our shores, and there is nothing that will leave a worse impression on the incoming immigrant than the treatment that is accorded to him on his arrival, and which has been mentioned by my hon. friend from Macdonald. I trust that action will be taken by the government in order to provide these people with proper accommodation, immediate action for the present year, as well as some provision in the supplementary estimates for providing public buildings for their accommodation in time to come.

I would like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche). I regret very much to have to criticise the action of the government which I am supposed to support : at the same time in this matter I believe they have been neglectful of their duty. What the hon. member for Macdonald has said is true enough, that this is not a new thing, it is not something that has come to the notice of the government for the first time. They have known that we were likely to have a hundred thousand Mr. ROCHE (Marquette).
people coming into the west this year. The prediction was made four or five years ago that the increase in the population of that country would double from year to year, as it has done in the United States, until possibly we should receive each year two hundred and fifty thousand people. I made that prediction myself some four years ago, and I said that it would come to pass within ten years. I still adhere to the prediction that within ten years from the date of that prediction we will have not less than 250,000 immigrants every year coming into Manitoba and the North-west Territories. The United States got this year alone, nearly 800,000 people, showing that the prediction I made is justified. When this was called to the attention of the government, a sum should have been put in the estimates to see that better accommodation was provided for these people when they arrive. The citizens of Winnipeg and of the province of Manitoba have to undergo a great deal of expense in connection with immigration. I left Winnipeg last Saturday. On Friday afternoon I attended a meeting of the general hospital board in the city of Winnipeg, and I found that on that day there were thirteen applications for private wards and many applications for the general wards of the hospital, which could riot be granted, as there was not accommodation for the patients who desired admission. That institution is largely supported by private contributions by the people of Winnipeg and of Manitoba. The legislature of Manitoba a few days ago voted $25,000 for the purpose of erecting a new wing to the hospital, and the work will be commenced within the next few days. A large part of the immigration is of no great benefit to Manitoba ; it merely passes through to the Territories, and the people of Winnipeg should not be called upon to take care of these immigrants. In one children's ward there were six small cots. I found that five of the occupants of these cots were foreigners, Icelandic, German, Polish, Russian and Scandinavian, who had been in the country but a short time. The support and care of those who are taken ill at the city of Winnipeg are being provided for by the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba. It is the duty of this government not only to take those people there, but to care for them after they arrive. There is nothing that will so quickly put a stop to this movement of immigration into Canada as to have the people write back to England that when they arrived on our shores they could find no place to rest their weary bones when illness came upon them. We are likely to have in the near future a very large influx of people from the British Islands. Those people who come from England especially, in my opinion, make poor pioneers. They are first class settlers, but they are poor pioneers in a new country. They are accustomed to

the comforts of a settled country, you will find them very headstrong and slow to adapt themselves to the conditions that they will find on the prairie. It is expected that quite a large percentage of the immigrants who will arive will be English colonists, and we are anxious that their first impression shall be favourable. Poor accommodation has been provided for these people as far as hospitals are concerned ; in fact scarcely anything has been done by the government. It is true that although the government have somewhat neglected the matter, they are at the same time not entirely to blame. We know that as a matter of fact other institutions, other corporations and private individuals have not been equal to the emergency that has taken place. We know that there is scarcely a wholesale man in the city of Winnipeg who has accommodation for the transaction of the business which has come to him. I left Winnipeg last Saturday, and on Friday I looked around the city and I found a great many cellars being blasted out preparatory to the erection of warehouses. Such firms as Greenshields, Son & Company, of Montreal, Which had no confidence in the west in years gone by, are there to-day, and in order to get ready for business as quickly as possible, they are having new cellars taken out by dynamite, and they are facilitating the work in every way. These corporations admit that they are not ready for this great rush of immigration, and it is therefore no wonder if the government find themselves in this position. The railway companies have been doing all they could to cope with this immigration, but it has come upon them with more rapidity than they anticipated. If this debate will bring out ail the facts, it will have a good effect, and we will forgive the government if they have been guilty of some dereliction in the past. I think it is the duty of the right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to find out what steps have been taken by the officials of the Interior Department to care for these people after they have arrived, to see that there shall be no distress among them ; to see that the sick shall be properly looked after, to see that every one upon arriving will be able to write a letter back home saying that he has been well treated. The policy in the city of New York, in years past, was, that whenever a certain number of immigrants of a desirable class had arrived there a guard was put in charge of eight or ten, and as long as they remained in New York city they were well cared for, and they were immediately asked to sit down and write a letter home to the village they came from describing the treatment they had received on their arrival in New York. If some of the immigrants who have arrived at Winnipeg were to write back home twenty-four hours after their arrival, I do not think they would write very' cheerful or encouraging 364
letters or letters which would induce many immigrants to come out. This has been the condition of affairs, but it should not he allowed to continue. The movement is now upon us. There is a very large military hall in the city of Winnipeg, and I submit that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) should be asked to give that hall, which will hold 400 immigrants, and which should have cots placed in it, and there should he a bus ready to convey immigrants from the depot to the hall. When I left there last Saturday I saw a large number of immigrants around the streets, who could not get work on account of the cold weather, as work had not begun, who could not get west, and who had no place to sleep. They went to the police station, they filled the wards of the station, and the Canadian Pacific Railway did what they never had to do before, they opened up their station and allowed them to sleep, not only in the ladies' and gentlemens' waiting rooms, but in the corridors, between the offices upstairs. I trust that the government, if they have not already done so, will take some steps to look after the 100,000 people which I expect will come to the west within the next four or five months. It is a very interesting calculation to know exactly the amount of rolling stock it is going to take to convey that number of people into that country within the next four or five months. If you will calculate the number of people to each car, say fifty to each, then calculate one carload of settlers effects for each family of five, then calculate that it requires from 7,000 to 10,000 feet of lumber to build each settler's house, then calculate the amount of food stuffs required for the year, as they will probably not raise food stuffs for the first year, you will find that they will require ns many cars to handle these people as have been necessary to haul out 35,000,000 bushels of wheat during the past five months, which means that the whole of the transportation facilities of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern in the west will be brought into requisition to transport .100,000 people within the next four or five months. So that the situation, if it is figured out in detail, becomes rather serious unless we get aid from some other quarters. I shall not say anything further at the present time upon the subject. Perhaps later on I shall go a little more fully into the figures, but in the meantime, 1 trust that the right hon. Prime Minister and the acting Minister of the Interior will give this subject their attention, and see if they cannot suggest some means of dealing with the situation as it has arisen.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with what has been said by the three previous speakers during the debate. It is a week since I drew the attention of the government to the matter of the

transportation of immigrants, and since that time those who were then in transit have arrived at their destination. The conditions which prevailed at that time were not improved during any part of the journey. They continued right through. At the end of this week there comes a second large contingent, and I hope that the hon. acting Minister of the Interior (Hon. Sir Wm. Muloek) will he able to inform us whether anything practical has been done, whether any engagements have been made on behalf of the railway company to remedy the matter so that it will not occur again In the transportation of these immigrants who are arriving at Halifax this week. I have before me a copy of the petition that has been forwarded to the hon. acting Minister of the Interior, the hon. Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding), and the Hon. Secretary of State (Hon. Senator Scott) from the hospital board of the city of Winnipeg, calling attention to the absolute urgency of getting some assistance from this government to enable them to take care of the patients. It states :
A large number of Its patients are from those who have recently arrived as immigrants in the province of Manitoba. Many of these come direct to the hospital from the immigration buildings in the city of Winnipeg.
2. For a long time the Dominion government made payments to the hospital in respect of immigrant patients on the basis of sixty cents per day for the time each patient was in the hospital and the government still requires the returns to be made out by the hospital in the same form but the grant that has been received for several years past is very much less than the amount so computed.
As a matter of fact, the amount paid by this government to the hospital per capita is growing less and less. Now, an appeal has been made for a substantial grant to help in the erection of a new building immediately. The case is urgent. There must be more hospital accommodation for these immigrants during the next few months, and as this petition has now been before the government for ten days or two weeks, I am in hopes that the acting Minister of the Interior will be able to tell us what conclusion has been come to in regard to it.

The subject which has been brought to our attention now, is one of very great importance and is deserving of the best consideration of both the House and of the government. If I heard correctly the contents of the article which my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) read from a newspaper, it described the state of affairs at the Winnipeg station. That portion of it wherein It described the busy scene, the quantities of baggage, the number of immigrants inquiring for information ; all that is very gratifying. It is also gratifying to find that our country is so attractive today, but it is to be regretted that, as in many other instances, there is a fly in the Mr. PUTTEE.
ointment, that the service is perhaps not adequate to the requirements.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has referred to the state of the hospital accommodation, and also to the facilities for railway transportation between Halifax and the west. I may say that I only to-day received the petition with reference to the hospital. I did not receive it ten days ago, but only about noon time to-day, and it took considerable time to read it. I have only this moment therefore been able to inform myself as to the nature of the demand made in that petition. The petition, which is dated, I think, on Friday last, asks for a grant of $50,000 towards the immediate erection of, I suppose, additional building, and also for some additional per capita allowance for patients in the hospital. That subject will at once receive the attention'of the government.
The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) called attention a few days ago to the inadequate facilities afforded by the Canadian Pacific Railway for the transportation of the immigrants. I immediately put myself in communication with the Canadian Pacific Railway authorities, and I am bound to confess that there was very substantial foundation for many of the statements made; apologetic explanations have been offered, but they are not adequate. I am in hopes that, with the arrival of the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Canada, all preventible oversights will disappear. At all events, after the Easter vacation, if there is any further ground of complaint, it will be my duty to make a frank statement to this House as to where any responsibility rests. I take no exception on this occasion that my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) has called the attention of the House to the alleged shortcomings of this government. It is his duty, and he is performing a public service. But he thinks that because in former years it was stated in the report that a large influx of American immigrants was expected, that therefore facilities should be on hand to-day to meet that anticipation. I have been in this parliament for twenty years or more, and I can remember anticipations of immigration yearly held out to us that were not afterwards realized. I have more confidence in our own anticipations now, but perhaps even those will not be realized. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) anticipates 100,000 immigrants this year. I trust that his anticipations may be realized, but lie tells us that his prophesy was for a period of ten years ; and if so. how does he account for it having been realized five years in advance ?
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Muloek).

speechtext: My prophesy was 250,000 immigrants within ten years, and it is coming to it each year.

I see. It is very safe to prophesy what will happen

five years hence. As to the lack of foresight on the part of the government, I have this to say : All the gentlemen who have spoken pointed out that others besides the government have failed in foresight. We are told that the business people of Winnipeg have not the facilities for transacting the business that has been thrown upon them by this immense immigration ; that the hotels are inadequate ; that the boarding houses are inadequate ; and we know that the railways are inadequate. Well, perhaps some little allowance may be made if the government is not wiser than those people to whom my hon. friends have referred. I am not able to speak by the book, except it be the blue-book of the Public Works department. I am not able to speak in detail as to whether the department has or has not anticipated this immigration. I am not familiar with the details of the working of either the Public Works Department or the Interior Department, and so I can only offer my explanations from such material as is to hand at the moment, and such as it is I will venture to offer it to the House by way of extenuation at least, and to show that we have not been absolutely wholly indifferent. I have here the report of the Minister of Public Works, which shows an expenditure of $1,700 during the fiscal year on immigration buildings in Winnipeg ; the erection of an immigration building at Calgary ; the erection of an immigration building at Lethbridge costing $4,000, another item of $1,400 for the erection of an immigration building at Saskatoon, and $1,500 for the erection of an immigration building at Strathcona. I presume that these are buildings for the purpose of meeting the requirements of the increased immigration. Therefore, some thought has been given to the future by providing these necessary buildings. I entirely sympathize with my hon. friends who urge that immigrants shall be furnished with every possible reasonable accommodation for their comfort, so that they may, with the least inconvenience, be able to start well in their new venture in life. It is of the utmost importance that these immigrants should receive a good impression of the country, and that they should find that the country, and the government representing the people, are not indifferent to their needs, but are ready to welcome them with open arms and extend to them excellent treatment. That is the duty of the government so far as it is possible to achieve it, and that duty the government will endeavour to perform. Until the House met this afternoon I was not aware that my hon. friend would bring this matter up. He was good enough to tell me of it a few moments before he took the floor, but that did not enable me to make any inquiries in the department of the Interior as to what arrangements are being made at the present time for the proper carrying on of the immigrant
business. I shall make it my duty to at once take steps to inform myself on these points; and what is more, I shall endeavour in all possible way to see that the immigrants are properly cared for. I am sure the whole resources of the country will be cheerfully placed at our disposal by parliament to do whatever is necessary to meet this large demand upon us ; a demand which is perhaps more than was expected. Indeed, I saw it stated in the papers yesterday that during the last week not less than 8,000 immigrants had arrived in Winnipeg-is that correct ?
Yes.

That is a very large number; it is over a thousand a day. Of course they are not going to stay in Winnipeg. An effort is made to distribute them. They come with more or less definite points of the country in view. They arrive at the sea ports; they perhaps rest there for a few hours, then they are carried by rail to the west. Some of them may get off by the way and become residents; but the great bulk are pushing on to the prairies. When they reach Winnipeg, the great mass of them, as the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) says, stop there only as transients, their ultimate object being to settle on the prairies. So that the facilities required at Winnipeg are only such as are necessary to meet the present occasion. It may be that the railways have not been able to carry the arriving streams of population as promptly as is desirable, and that this has caused a temporary congestion at Winnipeg, and possibly at other points. That isj incidental to our receiving such a large army of people as are now coming into the country. So that, while the government do not seek to avoid any* criticism, they expect that hon. gentlemen and the public generally will take a reasonable and fair view of the situation, and not give a black eye to the movement by overstating what may .be taking place. We are told that many of the immigrants who have arrived at Winnipeg have not been able to find beds, but have been obliged to sleep on the floor; and also that the hospital accommodation is inadequate. These are features of the situation to be regretted. Whilst I would not compare the hardships of the past with those of to-day, or suggest that these immigrants are having a softer time than our forefathers had, it is always well to bear in mind that there is always more or less discomfort connected with the movement of people from one country to another. I do not offer that as an apology for anything that is taking place, but as an explanation of these incidents which are more or less inseparable from the movements of people. Nevertheless, we must do all we can to afford reasonable shelter and comfort for these people, and reasonable facilities for them to get to their holdings ; and that I

pledge the House that the government will endeavour to do.
Mr. Speaker, I fear that the Iron. Postmaster General has too much on his hands. He has to take charge of the Minister of Agriculture's Department-
No.

And several other departments, and he has too much to do. But I would like him, when immigrants are coming in so fast just now, to direct some of them to the province of Ontario. In that province the farmers have not sufficient men to help them to doi their work. The stream of immigration seems to he all directed towards Manitoba and the North-west. Some lion, gentlemen say that the city of Winnipeg will get no benefit from the people who are going to the Northwest. I think AVinnipeg will get benefit from every one of them. Therefore I do not think the people of Winnipeg ought to object to putting up temporary buildings for these people. But what I would like the minister to do would be to help the farmers of Ontario to get some of this immigration. From 50,000 to 100,000 agricultural labourers could find employment and comfortable homes with the farmers of Ontario. We have great respect for Manitoba and the North-west: but they are not the only places in the world, and we expect the government to do something for us in Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, of course there may be conditions in the present situation which the government could not very well foresee; but I have not been able to gather from the remarks of the lion. Postmaster General that the government have done anything at all to provide for the condition of affairs which is now apparent at Winnipeg. The hon. gentleman states that there may have been some misgivings in the mind of the government as to the immigration that would flow into that country this year. We know that a very large immigration went in last year; and the government have officers there, and must have reasonably anticipated that there would be an enormous immigration both from the Dnited States and from Europe during the current! year. Any one who is familiar with the conditions in the west knows that delegations of farmers from the United States were going all through the western country last year for the purpose of locating lands with the idea of immigrating to this country; and in view of the magnificent crops of the past two years, a very large immigration should have been anticipated. Now. what have the government done according to the statement of the lion. Postmaster General, to meet the probable congestion in the city of Winnipeg ? Have they done anything at all ? Have they Sir WILLIAM MULOCK,
exercised ordinary business foresight ? Take the people of any city where a large number) of people are expected because of any unusual event, such as a great fair; we find them making provision to accommodate the people who are expected to come. Have the government done anything of this kind at Winnipeg ? I do not gather anything from the statement of the hon. Postmaster General to indicate that they have. It seems to me that it would have been a very easy matter for the government to have anticipated some considerable congestion at Winnipeg, and to have made arrangements through their officers, so that people need not be lying in police cells, in railway stations, and around the streets, at a time of the year when, according to my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), the weather is very inclement, and these people must have suffered considerably. A great deal depends on the impressions that are made on people who are coming in such large numbers to the country. If these people write to their friends in the countries from which they have come and detail the discomfort, the inconvenience and the suffering which they have experienced, it will counteract a great deal of the work of the immigration agents, and a great deal of the splendid impression which has been made throughout the world as to the future of that country, by reason of the great crops of the past two or three years. I agree with my hon. friend the Postmaster General in regard to one thing, and that is that it is the urgent and imperative duty of the government to remedy this state of things at once; they should have done so before. While my hon. friend has been very frank in admitting the faulty of the corporations and people that he is not concerned with, I think I may, on behalf of the government, admit that they; are to a great extent responsible for the present condition of affairs. AA^hile it may be true, ns my hon. friend says, that the conditions faced by these people may not be so severe as the conditions which were faced by the pioneeps of this country a hundred years ago. that does not as an argument amount to very much at all. What we have to do is to compare the conditions which the immigrants of to-day have to face not with the conditions of one hundred years ago. but with the 'conditions in the United States, our great competitor. I am very glad the matter has been brought to the attention of the House. We have a magnificent opnortnnitv at the present time to people the North-west country with the best class of settlers, and it will be a most regrettable thing, in the interest not only of the west but of the east, if anything should happen in the slightest degree to pxit a temporary check on the immigration now flowing into that country.

Margaree, N.S.-improvements, $800.
Will this complete the work ?
Yes.

I see in the Auditor General's Report, page Y-211 that a wharf was built at Margaree Island. Are those works close together ?
Mr. McLennan. They are twelve miles apart and separate works.
Meteghan Cove-restoration of breakwater, $2,300.
What is the proposed total expenditure ?
Five thousand three hundred dollars.
Will this be done by day's work or by tender ?
By day's work.
Why not by tender ?
Because it consists of general repairs, which can better be done by day's work.
How are the materials obtained ?
By the foreman of the work under the superintendence of the engineer.
Where is the resident engineer ?
The resident engineer is at Halifax.
You have all through the system a conductor and a foreman. What does the conductor really do ?
He buys the material and generally oversees the work.

He is down in the accounts for one hundred and fifty-nine days and the foreman is down for one hundred and twenty-two days. It would not take the^conductor one hundred and fifty-nine days to buy the materials.
I explained yesterday that the conductor bought the material and had charge of the whole work and kept the time, &c.
Is this a new system ?
No, that has been the system ever since our present engineer has been in office. So the chief engineer tells me.

Does the chief engineer report that it is necessary to have
a conductor as well as a foreman ? To an ordinary layman it would not seem that they were both necessary.
The chief engineer thinks it necessary to have a practical man continually at the work.

What is the conductor doing all the time.
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. He is time-keeper, and he has to purchase materials. There are a great many different kinds of materials required in these repairs, and the purchase of these, with time keeping and general charge and superintendence of the work should keep him pretty busy. He makes his report to the local engineer, who holds him responsible for the general condition of the works.

I should think the foreman, the practical man, would be held responsible for the conduct of the work. So, outside of the purchase of the material,
1 should think the foreman would have nothing to do but smoke or engage in some light occupation of that kind. Possibly there may be something else he has to do, but the minister seems to be as much puzzled to tell us what it is as we are to conjecture.

Seriously speaking, I think that probably the man put in charge of the work is a practical man, probably a carpenter. He could not be away from the work for the necessary time looking after men, and also purchasing the various materials required for these repairs, and, also act as foreman. Of course, if the local engineer resides there, he could do this. But the man in charge of a work like this could hardly be the foreman, unless he had also a business capacity, and then the work would probably suffer by his absence when buying material. I have had no experience, but the chief engineer tells me that it has been the practice of the department for many years to conduct these works in this way. I shall be pleased to look into this matter. If two men are unnecessary, there is no reason why one should not be dispensed with.
Who is the representative of the constituency in which this, work is ? I am afraid the hon. gentleman has been taking some lessons in Ontario.
1 think it is the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax).
Oh, no ; take that back.

L beg the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Ingram's) pardon. This is in the constituency of the leader of the opposition. If that lion, gentleman has been taking lessons in Ontario, I hope they have done him good.
I do not know wliat the hon. minister refers to: I have been talking about Meteghan for the last ten or fifteen minutes.
That was passed.

No, Mr. Chairman, you called ' passed ' just as I rose. You call 'passed' whenever there is an interval of five seconds, as it is your duty to do. But I have been reading from the Auditor General's Report about Meteghan, and that is what I have been discussing.
The MINISTER O# PUBLIC WORKS. There is a misunderstanding, then. In that case, I would say in answer to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) that the work is in Digby county.

The vote of last year Jf>3,000, and the vote of this year make a total of $5,300 for this work. According to the Auditor General's Report there is a conductor, 157 days at $2.50, and three foremen at $217.53 ; labourers, $1,437. No one will pretend to say that it requires three foremen and a conductor to carry on the work of that character.

No doubt, our engineer at Halifax allowed some men ten, fifteen or twenty-five cents a day more than the ordinary workmen making them foremen. But if on investigation we find that men are paid for services which they do not render, it may be well for us to consider whether we should not get somebody else to look after the work. I have not the slightest doubt, however, that the men called foremen in the accounts are practical men and give a faithful day's work for every day's pay they receive.
But we have an expenditure of over $2,000 say for foremen and labourers out of a total expenditure of $5,000. Will the hon. minister say that it requires that much 7

There is no such thing as three foremen on this work. The representative of the county has nothing to do with tile payment of the foremen. The engineer fixed the charges and appointed the men. The representative of a county lias nothing to do with the wages. I have never interfered with the engineer. He fixes the wages and pays the foremen what they are entitled to. At Meteghan, there is only one foreman, Mr. Robichaud. There is also a Mr. Deveau on the work, and they give him a little extra pay and call him a foreman of the men on the work. But I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) is entirely mistaken about three foremen.

If the hon. gentleman will refer to page V-213 of the Auditor General's Report he will see the figures. If there is Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
any fault, it is with the blue-books, not with us.
It is probable that one foreman was employed when the other was not.
Oh, yes. There were two different men-one left and the other took his place.
Is this work in the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Copp's) constituency ?
Yes. This work has been going on for four or five years. It is .an immense breakwater. The former breakwater went to destruction in a storm.
Has the hon. gentleman any idea when it will be completed 7
I believe it will be completed next year. I think it will require only about $3,000 more to build the work-that is about $3,000 more than what there is this year.
Why not get the total sum in this year 7
Because you could not spend it within a year. You can spend only about $3,500 or $4,000 on such a work as this within a year. You can only employ a certain number of men at one time.

There has been an explanation as regards the number of overseers, the explanation being that different men were employed at different times. But there is a matter that has not yet been explained and it is this. At page V-213 of the Auditor General's Report, we find that there has been a total expenditure on this work of $3,199.93. Of that total expenditure, $610 is spent for overseeing, independently of anything paid to the engineer. Is tiiis a fair proportion having regard to the total expenditure, and having regard also to the amount expended on "material and the amount expended on labour 7 Does it not come back to this proposition which we had before, that works carried on by day labour under the superintendence of the department cost vastly /more than' they would if the requirements of the statute were carried out and the work was let by tender 7 I have heard the explanation more than once on this subject of repairs. The case may be just as stated, but I must admit that I am not at all impressed as yet, with the argument that it is impossible to let these works partaking of the nature of repairs by tender. And I do submit that, these matters cropping up from time to time, whatever the department may have thought before, it is time they took this, as we say, into their serious consideration to see whether the time has not arrived when they should reconsider their position and adopt the spirit as well as the language of the statute and let these works by public tender
Will the hon. gentleman tell us how many workmen are employed on this work ?
I think about twenty or twenty-five men at one time.
Would the hon. gentleman state about how long they would be employed constantly ?
They go to work as early as they can in the summer after the vote is passed, and work until about Christmas, or until cold weather. Twenty-five men are not working every day.

I observe when I come to contrast the expenditure of overseeing and the labour with the cost of the material supplied, that the percentage of cost is enormously large in proportion to the amount of material used. The material for the breakwater cost $1,152.90, the overseeing and the labour cost $2,047.03. Now, as the work was all of the roughest possible character, handling cheap material in the cheapest fashion, it seems extraordinary that it cost $1.50 to use up a dollars worth of material. There is evidently something very far wrong.

They had to tear down the old work before they could repair it. In some places they have to go down seven or eight feet in the mud in order to make a foundation. It costs as much, and in some cases more, to tear down the old work than to build up the new. That is the reason why the labour costs more than the material.
What is the length of this work ?

It must be 1,200 or 1,400 feet long. I think they only tear down about eighty feet at a time. There is a tremendous tide there, and they can only take out a portion of the work at a time and build it up as fast as they take it out; otherwise they would lose all their work.
Necum Teuch-wharf, $3,000.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). Is this being done by tender ?
No, by day labour.
Why do you do it by day labour, contravening the statute ?
I do not see that it is contravening the statute.

Does the Minister of Public Works not know that there is in an Act of parliament a provision that requires all works costing $5,000 or over to be tendered for ? And there must be an Order in Council to the same effect.

I do not think my hon. friend, who ought to be well versed in the Act, is quoting it correctly. At the time this work was started there was a provision by Order in Council for expending amounts under $5,000.
I understood the minister to say that he is asking for $5,000 for this year.
The total is $5,000. There seems to be some new theory about the interpretation of the statute. Perhaps we might as well have it from the hon. gentleman.

As I understand the law, I think there is a provision in it that if the officers of the department think a work can be more advantageously done by day labour than by tender, it can be done by day labour. The Order in Council to which I refer was, I think, in existence for eighteen or twenty years, but two or three months ago it was referred to the Justice Department and declared ultra vires. So we do not take advantage of that Order in Council any more. Perhaps if it is found in the public interest to have some provision made for expending small amounts, there will have to be some amendment made to the Act. There is a provision in the Act under which the technical officers of the department are to carry on works of considerable extent by day labour, so far as they can do so in the public interest.

There is no such a tiling in the statute. The statute provides that in an extraordinary case, where, for instance, the banks of a canal burst away and it is impossible to let out work by tender, it may be done by day labour under the charge of the department, and the minister, on a report of council, may get authority from council to do the work by day labour in an exceptional case like that. But the statute and the Order in Council apply to all work costing over $5,000.

The hon. gentleman is a practical man, and no one in this House knows better than he does the difficulty of carrying on work similar to the one discussed a few minutes ago, a wharf 1,500 feet long, requiring two or three thousand dollars to repair it, where it has to be thrown down in order to find out what is wrong. That could not be done by contract.

Why does the hon. gentleman argue contrary to the law ? Parliament in its wisdom passed a statute by which it is requisite that all sums over

a certain amount should be expended in a certain manner. That law must be obeyed until it is changed.

We had better have that point settled by the Minister of Justice, so that we may not go on spending so much of the people's money without knowing what we are doing. It used to be generally understood when hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition, that the law required all sums over $5,000 to be expended by contract. Now that they are in control, there is an ' if ' about it. If there is an ' if ' about it, I think that we should have it understood before we go any further. To my mind it is absurd to say that you cannot get material by contract. You have a gentleman perambulating the country at a time when it is utterly impossible to get timber and material for repairing a dock at the price you could get it for if the work was let by contract, and in a season when the timber was available. That is what a business man would do in the section of the country where I live. But instead of that, as I understand the hon. gentleman, you have a gentleman running around the country buying material at a time of the year when it should be on the spot and when the work should be progressing. If it is necessary for you to get your timber by contract, the engineers must know pretty nearly what is required, and if the amount is not quite sufficient it is easy to procure the balance. But I am satisfied in my own mind that it is a wrong principle to have a man running round the country buying timber when the timber could be got out by contract and on the spot. Why has that change come about in the hon. gentleman's mind ? I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce sitting there complacently. He don't say a word. He used to be very loud in his denunciation of the way money was being expended without contract when he was on this side of the House. How things have changed ! He sits there complacently and sees the law violated without saying a word. His hand is not lifted with holy horror now, we hear none of those thunder-tones we used to hear when he was in opposition, everything now is lovely, although they are violating a statute just as flagrantly as they said the Conservatives used to do when a Conservative government was in power.
Neil's harbour-breakwater, $4,000.
This is in the county of Victoria. The total cost of this breakwater is .$18,000. and this sum will complete the work. It is a new work, now under contract.
The contractors belong to the city of Ottawa, Heney and Smith.

I find that this harbour was up last session and that $14,000 was voted for it. The hon. Minister of Public Works said it was then under contract for $14,000. What is the explanation of the further vote of $4,000 ?
There must be some mistake, because the amount of the contract was $16,600. It was made on the 29th November, 1901. There may have been a mistake in taking down the figures in ' Hansard.'
Perhaps the hon. member for Victoria will tell us something about that work.

Neil's Harbour is one of the most important fishing stations in my county. A large number of fishermen came over from Newfoundland and settled in that place, bringing a larger class of boats with them than our fishermen used to have. They have to go to deep water to get the cod-fish and the great trouble was that whop stormy weather would come on they would have to throw out their ballast, get all the men they could together to get their boats hauled up on shore and wait until the stormy weather would be over. This breakwater is not yet completed. I used to growl considerably because the contractors were not asked to complete the work within the time which was specified in the contract, but when completed it will be of immense value to a large number of fishermen in that locality. They will be able to moor their boats inside this breakwater during all seasons as safely as if they had been in the shelter which is in the Ottawa river. It will be of immense benefit to that class of people. I may say in connection with contracts that except in perhaps one or two instances where repairs have been made, I have insisted in every case that everything in my county should be put up to tender and contract. It is a great relief to myself and, I think, in the end more satisfactory to every one.
Would the hon. minister give us the date of the contract and the amount ?
The 29th November, 1901, is the date, and the amount of the contract'is $16,600.

We get from that an explanation of how this money is expended. Last year the hon. minister came down and asked for $14,000. It appears that at that time he had already let a contract which was to cost $16,600. That is an explanation to the committee. The policy of the government seems to be that after they have let a contract for $16,600, they will come to the House and ask for $14,000. and the House expects naturally that that sum will complete the work ; yet, the government know that they have already let a contract that will cost $2,600 more than they asked

the House to vote. Surely that Is not good policy. That accounts for these extra votes. We voted $14,000 last year and now the department comes forward and asks the committee for $4,000, when they knew last year what the contract price was.

That has not been the policy of the government, and it will not be in future. It may be that the hon. minister explained when he was asking for the $14,000, that that was all he expected to spend during the fiscal year. There can be no reason why full Information should not have been given at that time in regard to this vote, because the contract was then made.

We will have it out with the hon. Minister of Public Works in reference to the meaning of the statute as to his power to have work done by day labour :
The minister shall invite tenders, by public advertisement, for the execution of all works, except in case of pressing emergency-
Such as a canal being broken down.
-in which delay would be injurious'to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
Hear, hear.

That only applies to the staff you have on the work. Suppose the Lacliine canal staff were employed all winter for the purpose of making repairs on the ground that it could be more economically and expeditiously done; that would be in keeping with the application and the sole application of the statute. You have no right to employ for a work costing over $5,000 a staff outside of the department or to hire men for the purpose of doing it. That is in direct contravention to the statute.
Where does my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) get the limit of $5,000 ?
That is mentioned somewhere in the Act.
No, it is not.
The limitation is in the Order in Council.
Which was illegally passed.

This statute applies to all work. It has no limitation at all. There is an Order in Council; I suppose that the hon. gentlemen at present governing the country have come to the conclusion that it is nlti'a vires, that it has no application at all, and not binding on the government.
However, this clause applies to all work, it has no limitation. The limitation of $5,000 was probably in the Order in Council but the application of the clause in the statute is general.

I think after the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has read the Act, those who have listened to it will agree that I gave a very fair explanation of what the Act meant.
I still hold that the interpretation I put upon it is correct and that in doing work, such as most of those which have been under discussion, the day's labour plan is the only practical business way in which it can be done.
We are not arguing that part of it. We are arguing the meaning of the statute.
My hon. friend takes one view and other hon. gentlemen take another view.
I would like to know the other hon. gentlemen, in addition to myself, who take that view. Does the hon. Minister of Justice agree with it ?

The Minister of Justice agrees with me. What I want to point out to the hon. gentleman is that when people differ as to the interpretation of an Act of parliament they must depend on the highest court of appeal and the hon. gentleman will find that the Auditor General takes that view and we will have to abide by his decision. If he comes to the decision that my hon. friend puts the proper interpretation on the_statute we will then have to have legislation.
I think if the hon. Minister of Public Works will look at the overrulings of the treasury report in the Auditor General's Report, he will find that the Auditor General does not take that view.

The Auditor General was acting on an ultra vires Order in Council.
New Campbellton-ballast wharf, $5,000.

This is a revote. The coal company owns a wharf there which is in a very bad state of repair and it was represented that the department should repair that wharf. The department would not spend money on the property unless it was transferred to the Crown, and as that question was not settled no expenditure was made. I understand that now the manager of the company is willing to transfer the old wharf to the Crown if we will take charge of it.
What will be the total expenditure ?
The chief engineer estimates that to put the old wharf in good shape it will cost $11,500.
What is the necessity for the work ?

This is a large coal shipping station and the practice of vessels coming there has been to throw out their ballast in places where it was calculated to injure the harbour. This ballast wharf will not only give deeper water but it will afford a good deal of shelter and will enable vessels to put their ballast in the pier. Something of that kind was done at North Sydney a year or two ago.

It would seem rather to be an expensive way of preventing vessels throwing out ballast in improper places. In most ports, vessels in discharging their ballast, are subject to a harbour by-law and are punished for violating that law. Is there a real necessity for this work for the purpose of shelter.
As a rule this is a fair harbour, but in south-east and southerly winds this pier will afford shelter to a small class of vessels which would be on the inside.
Are there coal mines near there ?
There are coal mines there in active operation and they have been shipipng for years.
Is this work being done by tender and contract ?

No action has been taken yet, but it will be done by tender.
New Harbour-breakwater repairs, protection slopes, &c., $1,500.

It is hardly to be expected that the minister can supervise every expenditure in a large department like that of Public Works, but the Auditor General's report shows that this is a case that out Herod's Herod, and one that is calculated to make the members of the Ontario government feel ill at ease in thinking that other people can surpass them in this kind of thing. The Auditor General tells us that there was an expenditure last year of $3,700, and that it cost $308 for overseers and timekeepers to supervise an expenditure of $1,200 in wages. There were about a dozen workmen on the job. We first had Mr. Patterson engaged for 47 days at $3 a day, to overlook these dozen men, and as if Mr. Patterson was not enough, a gentleman named Gillis was appointed to help him as overseer. One would think that these two could look after the dozen workmen, but it would seem that the department wanted a third man to superintend the other two superintendents, and so a gentleman named Sangster was brought in as book-keeper.
But that is not all. There was a small quantity of material to be purchased, and a gentleman named Kirk was commissioned to do that.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) will look into that account he will probably find that these gentlemen were not all occupied at the same time.

The Auditor General's report shows that Mr. Patterson is a foreman and that Mr. Gillis is a sub-foreman, so that there could be no conflict of authority between the two, and one gets paid for 47 days and the other for 44 days. Mr. Sangster was also occupied for 44 days, so that the evidence is that the three were occupied at the same time. The whole thing seems to have been carried out on a scale that would do credit to a Tammany ring. There was a foreman, a sub-foreman, and a time-keeper to watch twelve workmen, and as if these three men could not find time to buy the materials, Mr. Kirk got a commission of 5 per cent to do so. In what riding is this? Who represents it? Who is this Jack the Ripper or Dick Turpin of Canadian politics who is making such raids on the public exchequer ?

The criticism of my hon. friend is hardly fair. I am willing to admit that probably it is difficult to explain the items as they are given in the Auditor General's report. If any such state of affairs existed in the carrying on of these works as the hon. gentleman describes, it is time we had a change in the men who had charge of this department. I am satisfied that it is quite a mistake. The work is in the county of Guys-borough.
Oh.

The only gentleman who came to the rescue last year in connection with this vote was the hon. member from Guysborough. Here is what the Minister of Public Works said on this matter then, and it is interesting:
MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. We had some little doubt about this place a couple of years ago. I must admit it was difficult for us that night to put our finger on the very point where New Harbour was located. The coast of Nova Scotia is very wide and long and my colleague and myself had some trouble before we could lay our finger on that spot, but we found it easily after the money was voted and spent.

There ought be some explanation of this. There is no doubt that from the Auditor General's Report the two foremen and the time keeper were employed at the same time and practically during the same number of days. Here we have a cost of $7 a day for superintending the expenditure of $20 a day in wages. Surely one of these men might have been

spared to go and purchase $1.80 worth of galvanized buckets or five kegs of nails and spikes: yet the department employed this man ICirk specially to make these little purchases. 1 think the minister should tell us that he intends to keep both eyes on this riding of Guysborough this year. It was only two years ago that an expenditure was to be made in this same riding, and they were unable to find the place; and you have the fact staring the House in the face today that about as many men are employed to look after the employees as the men employed.
My hon. friend will see that there was a good carpenter employed at $2 a day, though he is called a sub-foreman.
Is it the policy of the department to pay five per cent on these purchases ?
No commissions are allowed.
The hon. minister will find, at page 214 of the Auditor General's Report, that commissions have been paid.

It would not be an unreasonable rate of commission if this man was employed to purchase something for the department and turn it in at cost price. But certainly that is not the general policy of the department.
Mi-. BENNETT. It does not appear that this.is the case at all. I assume that the prices for the things purchased were fair and reasonable. I do not know who this Mr. Kirk is; but his purchases extend from buckets to cement and spruce, so that if he deals in all these things he must be engaged in a large way in business. The inference is that he purchased them and was allowed five per cent commission on them.

I will explain the matter. Mr. Kirk lives in the county of Antigonish, about sixty miles from the place where the articles were to be delivered, and it is difficult to get them delivered at this poiut, which is on the sea coast. I have no doubt the department got this man to make the purchases, that they were made at as low a rate as they could be got at, and that they allowed him a commission of five per cent.

I suppose that what took place was that certain articles were purchased from Mr. Kirk, and that he purchased a number of articles which he had not in stock, and was allowed five per cent upon them. I know that what my hon. friend says is correct, that Antigonish is at a considerable distance from this point.
Ogden's Pond-to complete channel protection work, $650.
Does this complete the work ?

Yes.
Petit de Grat-reconstruction of protection work and dredging, $5,000.
Does this complete the work, and is it let by tender or contract ?
We have just advertised for tenders for this work; it will be done by contract. The estimated cost is $6,600.

What is it-a work to make the harbour more efficient and more sheltered ?
The SIINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, it is a new channel to be opened up, protected by cribwork, instead of the present channel. It is a protection harbour, principally for fishing boats.
Poirierville-wharf, $3,500.

This work is now under contract. The amount of the contract is $4,388. This vote will complete the work. It is to provide a safe harbour for a thickly-settled district.
Port George-breakwater, $3,500.
Is this a new work ?

It is not a new' work. It is an extension of the pier and breakwater. It is done by day labour.
Port Hastings-wharf, $4,000.

This is a revote. No site has been procured yet. The question of a site has been under negotiation. The work will be done by tender and contract.
Port Hawkesbury-wharf, $8,200.
As to both of these wharfs, the one that has just been passed and this one, I would like the minister to state why it is necessary for the government to build these wharfs.
