There are from $5,000 or $6,000 paid in bounties to fishermen in that locality, and there are large business firms curing and bringing fish and bringing ships from the ocean to carry out the products of the fishermen. Last fall, during the month of October, three large ships came there to load fish to take away to the European markets. These ships generally come late in the season.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman's observation throws some light on the subject. One of the reasons he gives is rather novel, that is, that a large sum is paid out in fishing bounties. I was not aware before that it was necessary to build wharfs to pay out these fishing bounties. I thought that as soon as the bounties were earned, there would be no difficulty in finding the earners of them.
* Mr. TURGEON. The large amount of the fishing bounties paid in the locality is an evidence of the large extent of the fishing industry there.
How far is Shippegan harbour from Shippegan wharf ?

About five miles. Shippegan harbour, or Shippegan gully connects the Gulf of St. Lawrence with the Baie des Chaleurs. A few years ago Shippegan harbour, by the special works which have been carried on, was dredged to a sufficient depth to enable the Caraquet fleet, consisting of some 200 or 300 vessels, going to the fishing banks, to pass that way, instead of going around Mascou Island, and thus to save some fifty miles. This is a great saving of time and hardship to our fishermen in carrying on their most patriotic industry, and the amount of money spent is nothing compared with the advantage it confers. I think this parliament never votes any money of greater public advantage than the money voted for the improvement of our coasts in the maritime provinces.
Did I understand the minister to say that the contract for this wopk is $13,000 ?

The contract price is $12,000. The total cost of the work is estimated to be $14,350, the sum over the contract being for superintendence and contingencies.
Upper Salmon river-Alma pier, $4,000 .

This work is under contract. The total cost is $5,750. We only expect to pay out during

the present fiscal year $1,750, so we are asking a revote of $4,000. The contract was let on the 6th August, 1902.
Harbours and rivers. Maritime provinces generally-generally repairs and improvements, $20,000.

I find that the usual vote of $15,000 for the maritime provinces is too small as it has obliged men to go without pay and accounts to be carried over to the next year. I think it is better to ask for the amount really required, and for that reason I ask that the vote be increased by $5,000.
What class of work is intended to be done ?

This is for emergency repairs on the report of the engineers, caused principally by damage from storms-unforeseen accidents of one kind and another, which my bon. friend will know are very general in those waters.
Harbours and rivers, Ontario-Amherstburg- dredging, $5,000.
This is a revote, for the same reason that exists in some other cases, that we had no available dredge.
Where is this dredging done ?	*
It has not been done because we had no dredge to do the work. This year we hope to have a dredge.
Where in the Detroit river do you propose to do the work ?
From the main channel into the wharf at Amherstburg.
And it is a work of great importance.

I understand the hon. gentleman to say that this is a revote, because the department has not been able to get a dredge to do the work. But there is a very good dredge which could be had and which did work last year and the year before for the Department of Public Works. The Chatham Dredging Company have a dredge which did good work at the mouth of the Thames and also at Rondeau harbour, and I think there is little doubt that it can perform the work satisfactorily. And the company are prepared to do it cheaper than the department can have it done for by its own dredges.
I am pleased to have that information. We will have the matter inquired into and ascertain whether the dredge which the hon. gentleman refers to is capable of doing the work.

This same dredging company did work very satisfactorily at Rondeau and at the mouth of the Thames.
I appeal to the ex-Minister of Public Works whether that was not the case.

No doubt the dredge referred to did good work, but I am not quite sure that it would be capable of doing the work at Amherstburg. I think that the bottom there is very hard. The American government are carrying out large dredging work in the river just opposite Amherstburg. I may say that Amherstburg has lost a very important coal trade because the depth of the water is not sufficient, and I would urge upon my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works the great importance of having this dredging done. There are American dredges available, but when the government employ American dredges reproaches are levelled against it. I think, however, that when a work is urgent we would be justified in employing foreign dredges and admitting them in bond. Of course the work to be carried out at Amherstburg would cost a larger amount of money than the $5,000 in the estimates. I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to give his special attention to this Amherstburg work. I have visited the place and know the facts well.

I would like the Minister of Public Works, in view of what the exMinister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has said, whether he has a report of the engineer as to the character of the soil or the material to be removed.
Clay, hard-pan, boulders and rock. This work my hon. friend says will cost $25,000.

I think that $14,000 or $15,000 would dredge the channel along the wharfs and be sufficient for the needs of the moment, but to complete the work and make it a good job, it would be necessary to spend $2o,000 to $30,000.
Has anything been done to remove the boulders spoken of last year.

No.
Barrie, Ont.-construction of wharf, $3,000.

This is an item which has been in the estimates for a number of years. I am not going at all to discuss the policy, but I wish to call the hon. minister's attention to this fact. The town of Barrie is not in the riding I represent, and I see that the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is not present, but I have what appears to me good and sufficient reasons for calling not only the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works, but incidentally the attention of the ex-Minister of Public Works to this item. About a year ago there



was a good deal of correspondence between the mayor of tbe town of Barrie and the hon. member for North Simcoe on this question. I do not mean to say that many letters passed between them, but such letters as did pass and were published in the press were long and moderately warm, and the position was this. Each one was blaming the other for the delay that had occurred. I think I am entitled to rise to a question of privilege upon this matter, because I was dragged into it also. In my innocence of parliamentary procedure, having an office in the town of Barrie and having been a ratepayer in the north riding of Simcoe for many years, and having been asked frequently by a number of residents in the town, with reference to this wharf, I ventured to write to the then Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) asking him to have it built in the near future. I think it is a work very much in the interest of the fishermen. Sometimes a schooner comes in but hardly any large vessels come in there. This is quite a fishing centre, but, if the fishermen have no place to shelter their boats in a storm, it would be impossible to carry on that industry.

Then, according to the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Deputy Speaker's) statement, we have a pier intended for the fishermen, yet the fishermen cannot get at it until the bar is dredged. But there is no money for dredging purposes.

speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the dredging would take place as soon as the wharf was finished.

If the hon. minister is going to build wharfs and do dredging for the fishermen of Bayfield, I can draw his attention to Port Bruce which is quite as important. We have just as many fishermen at Port Bruce as they have, and I question if we have not more, and the revenue is probably larger.
It is always calm weather at Port Bruce.

We all know that a good many works of this kind were commenced under very different conditions from those which prevail now, at a time when there was a considerable shipping business at these points. We must recognize that many of those works have fallen into disuse, and 1 think no more money should be spent on them. I acknowledge that both parties have offended in that respect. But this is a notable case, and I appeal to the hon. gentleman whether we should enter upon a course of that kind in view of the increasing demands from all quarters of Canada for public works far more necessary. It is a question whether we should spend any more money in keeping up breakwaters and docks that were built many years ago, when the original need of constructing those works has entirely ceased to exist. Of course there will always be a pressure to keep them up, and there will always be these recurring accidents of the harbours filling up with sand, and small fishing vessels may still require to come into those harbours. But I submit that we have reached the period when we might consider on both sides of the House whether it is

wise in tlie interest of the country, to continue to build works of that sort.
